claims.text: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by the nanoscale precipitate phase.
A uniform nanoscale precipitate distribution promotes crack blunting.
A uniform nanoscale precipitate distribution promotes crack deflection.
Crack blunting and deflection impede crack propagation.
The proposed initial material has a nominally single-phase, such as FCC, matrix containing a small volume fraction of nanoscale precipitates.
Controlled heat treatment can modify precipitate size and volume fraction.
Uniform, finely dispersed precipitates act as obstacles to crack propagation.
Optimizing precipitate size and distribution will maximize precipitate-mediated toughening.
A substantial reduction in precipitate density will impair toughness.
Relative to the baseline, a fine and uniform precipitate distribution will increase fracture toughness.
Relative to the baseline, a fine and uniform precipitate distribution will produce more pronounced crack deflection.
Coarser or substantially fewer precipitates will produce lower toughness than a fine, uniform precipitate distribution.
The proposed mechanism should dominate in high-entropy alloys having a stable, nominally single-phase matrix.
The proposed mechanism should apply only over temperatures and loading conditions under which the precipitates remain thermally stable and do not significantly coarsen.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to multiphase or inherently brittle alloy systems.
Composition may modulate the influence of precipitates on toughness.

A lack of statistically significant toughness improvement and demonstrable crack deflection in the fine-precipitate condition relative to both baseline and coarse-precipitate conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
